description_full: Biogen Inc. discovers, develops, manufactures, and delivers therapies in the United States, Europe, Germany, Asia, and internationally. The company provides TECFIDERA, VUMERITY, AVONEX, PLEGRIDY, and TYSABRI for multiple sclerosis (MS); SPINRAZA for spinal muscular atrophy; SKYCLARYS to treat Friedreich's Ataxia; QALSODY for treating amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; FUMADERM to treat plaque psoriasis; BENEPALI, an etanercept biosimilar referencing ENBREL; IMRALDI, an adalimumab biosimilar referencing HUMIRA; FLIXABI, an infliximab biosimilar referencing REMICADE. It offers LEQEMBI for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease; ZURZUVAE for the treatment of postpartum depression; RITUXAN to treat non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), rheumatoid arthritis, two forms of ANCA-associated vasculitis, and pemphigus vulgaris; RITUXAN HYCELA for non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and CLL; GAZYVA to treat CLL and follicular lymphoma; OCREVUS for relapsing MS and primary progressive MS; LUNSUMIO to treat relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma; glofitamab for aRelapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; and other anti-CD20 therapies. Biogen Inc. has collaboration and license agreements with Merz Therapeutics; Alkermes Pharma Ireland Limited; Denali Therapeutics Inc.; UCB; Eisai Co., Ltd.; Genentech, Inc.; Neurimmune SubOne AG; Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc.; Samsung Bioepis; and Sage Therapeutics, Inc., as well as collaborations with Stoke Therapeutics, Inc. for the development and commercialization of zorevunersen, a disease modifying medicine for the treatment of Dravet syndrome; Dayra Therapeutics, Inc. to develop oral macrocyclic peptides; Vanqua Bio, Inc. for developing Vanqua's preclinical oral C5aR1 antagonist compound; City Therapeutics, Inc. to develop select novel RNAi therapies; and ALTEOGEN Inc. to develop subcutaneous (SC) formulations of biologics utilizing ALT-B4. The company was founded in 1978 and is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Biogen Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $36.7B market cap on $9.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 88% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $2.1B in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.71× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.8×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 42% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 0.63, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.03 vs 5y 0.50), so read it loosely.

Multiples send mixed signals against Healthcare peers: cheaper on P/FCF 17.9 vs 23.7, richer on P/E 107.5 vs 25.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 100% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 32 covering analysts target $265 on average, 7% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 0pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.47).
It runs a 88% gross margin and converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.71x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 18.0% of revenue on R&D and 2.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.4x net debt to EBITDA ($1.3B of cash against $6.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.8x.
Working capital ties up about 313 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.9% over 3 years, -6.0% over 5 years and -0.8% over 10 years, so the decline is easing, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 8.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -11.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: deferred revenue down 54% and 29 active clinical trials.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 3 sales over the past year, net $771K sold.
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 7,500 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 3.5x the Healthcare median, and productivity has risen 5.2% a year.
